Armour
AR-mur
n. (defensive equipment worn in battle; rendering Hebrew keli, nesheq, Greek panoplia, hopla)
From Old French armeure, Latin armatura. The KJV spelling keeps the British form. The key Greek term is panoplia — pan, all, and hopla, arms: the full kit, not a selection from it.

Biblical Definition

Armour is defensive equipment, and Scripture's two great passages on it teach opposite halves of one lesson. The first is negative. Saul dresses David in royal armour before Goliath, and David takes it off: “I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them” (1 Samuel 17:39). Untested armour is worse than none, and borrowed armour fits no one. The second is positive and is the Christian's standing order: “Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11), repeated for emphasis at verse 13 with the purpose stated three times over — to withstand, to stand, and having done all, to stand. It is worth noticing what the armour is for. It is not issued for advance, conquest, or victory; the verb Paul chooses is stand, because the victory has been won and the believer's task is to hold ground already taken. Every piece is a doctrine or a duty — truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God — so the man who neglects doctrine is not merely uninformed but unarmoured. Paul's other image supplies the ethical dimension: “The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light.” (Romans 13:12). Armour is put on the way clothing is put on, deliberately, daily, and by the man himself.

Webster 1828 Definition

Defensive equipment. David refuses Saul's untested armour; Paul commands the whole armour of God, whose stated purpose is not conquest but standing; Romans calls holiness itself the armour of light.

expand to see more

ARMOR, ARMOUR, n. [L. armatura.] Defensive arms; any habit worn to protect the body in battle; formerly called harness.

2. Steel or iron covering, either wrought into a coat of mail, or in plates.

3. In Scripture, the whole apparatus of defence appointed for the Christian soldier. Eph. 6.

4. Armor-bearer, one who carries the armor of another; an office of trust in the Hebrew armies.

5. Figuratively, whatever defends or protects; as the armor of light. Rom. 13.

Key Scripture

Ephesians 6:11 — "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil."

Ephesians 6:13 — "Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand."

Romans 13:12 — "The night is far spent, the day is at hand: let us therefore cast off the works of darkness, and let us put on the armour of light."

1 Samuel 17:39 — "And David girded his sword upon his armour, and he assayed to go; for he had not proved it. And David said unto Saul, I cannot go with these; for I have not proved them. And David put them off him."

Modern Corruption

The armour of God is treated as a devotional ritual to be recited each morning rather than as the doctrines and duties it names — and the word whole is quietly dropped, leaving Christians who have selected the pieces they like.

expand to see more

Ephesians 6 is often taught as a visualisation: picture the helmet, picture the breastplate, name each piece aloud. The passage itself names concrete realities. The girdle is truth — actual doctrinal truth known and held. The breastplate is righteousness, which in Paul means both Christ's imputed righteousness and the practising of it. The shoes are the preparation of the gospel of peace, meaning readiness to carry it. The sword is the word of God, which cannot be wielded by a man who has not learned it. To recite the list without acquiring the things is to mime putting on equipment one does not own. The Puritans understood this and wrote at length on each piece as a doctrine to be studied; William Gurnall's treatment runs to well over a thousand pages, because the armour is the Christian faith itself and not a morning liturgy.

The other loss is the word whole. Paul says panoplia twice, the full kit, and the pieces are not optional or interchangeable. A believer may take a genuine interest in truth and neglect righteousness, or hold sound doctrine and never lift the shield of faith, and the gaps are exactly where the wiles of the devil are aimed. There is a related and opposite error in the deliverance-ministry treatment of the passage, which reads the armour as a formula conferring protection by recitation. Paul locates the danger in wiles — stratagems, deceits — and the defence in doctrine known and obeyed, which is why the sword is the word and not an incantation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew keli (vessel, implement, hence weapons) and nesheq (equipment, armoury); Greek panoplia (full armour, from pan + hopla) and hopla (arms, instruments).

expand to see more

Hebrew keli (H3627) — article, vessel, implement; used of weapons and armour, and of the vessels of the sanctuary.

Hebrew nesheq (H5402) — equipment, weaponry, an armoury; used of Hezekiah's house of armour in Isaiah 39:2.

Greek panoplia (G3833) — full armour, the complete equipment of a heavy infantryman; used in Ephesians 6:11, 13 and Luke 11:22.

Greek hopla (G3696) — arms, instruments, weapons; the word in Romans 13:12 rendered armour and in 2 Corinthians 10:4 rendered weapons.

Greek thorax (G2382) — breastplate; the piece named for righteousness in Ephesians 6:14 and for faith and love in 1 Thessalonians 5:8.

Usage

"“The whole armour of God” — panoplia, the full kit; the pieces are not optional."

"“Having done all, to stand” — the armour is issued for holding ground, not for taking it."

"“I have not proved them” — David refuses equipment he has not tested, and kills the giant with what he has."
